citations: The group of patients with partial DPD deficiency represented a total of 580 patients, including 134 wild-type patients (*DPYD*1/*1*) and 446 patients harboring at least one genetic variant (208 patients carried one genetic variant and 238 patients more than one).

The remaining 2392 patients exhibiting normal DPD activity include 623 wild-type patients (*DPYD*1/*1*) and 1769 mutated patients in which a total of 3183 genetic variants were identified (831 carrying a single genetic variant and 938 carrying more than one).
All patients included in this study were eligible for an uracil analog-based chemotherapy (Supplementary Table S1).
As expected, our data showed a significant association between each of these genetic variants and low DPD activity (Fig. 1).

summary.summary:
## Background
Fluoropyrimidines (5‑FU/capecitabine) are widely used but can cause severe, sometimes fatal, toxicity in patients with reduced dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) activity. This study sequenced DPYD (exons and splice junctions) in 2,972 patients and related genotype to pretreatment DPD phenotype using the dihydrouracil/uracil ([UH2]/[U]) plasma ratio (partial deficiency defined as ≤10).

## Key Findings
- Established high‑risk alleles were strongly associated with lower DPD activity: DPYD*2A (c.1905+1G>A), DPYD*13 (c.1679T>G), and c.2846A>T (all P ≤ 0.001–0.0001 vs wild‑type).
- Several common variants showed only modest effects: hapB3 (c.1236G>A), c.496A>G (p.Met166Val), and DPYD*6 (c.2194G>A) were more frequent in patients with partial DPD deficiency, but the effect sizes were small relative to the high‑risk alleles.
- Rare/very rare DPYD variants (MAF <1%) were enriched in patients with low DPD activity:
  - Any rare variant: 9.3% (deficient) vs 3.2% (normal); P < 0.00001.
  - After excluding the three clinically established high‑risk alleles: 4.5% vs 2.6%; P < 0.03.
  - Restricting to rare variants predicted deleterious (CADD >15): 4.2% vs 1.6%; P < 0.001.
- Multiple novel or very rare putative loss‑of‑function variants (e.g., frameshift, stop‑gain, canonical splice) were identified in individuals with low DPD activity. All rare variants detected were heterozygous.

## Clinical Implications
- Beyond guideline variants (DPYD*2A, DPYD*13, c.2846A>T, and hapB3), rare deleterious DPYD variants contribute meaningfully to reduced DPD activity. Comprehensive DPYD sequencing can improve identification of patients at risk for fluoropyrimidine toxicity versus targeted SNP panels alone.
- Continue to apply CPIC/EMA dose reductions for established high‑risk alleles; interpret common variants with modest effects (e.g., hapB3, c.496A>G, DPYD*6) cautiously given smaller impact.
- Consider integrating NGS‑based genotyping with DPD phenotyping where available to optimize safety. Note: this study used DPD activity as a surrogate; prospective linkage to clinical toxicity is still needed.
